strengths: The paper identifies a useful, concrete failure mode in visual GUI agents: executing a toggle command even when the requested state already holds. Pairing change-state and preserve-state instructions provides a meaningful diagnostic beyond conventional click grounding.

The reported improvements are substantial across four agents. Table 1 shows O-AMR increasing from 43.95% to 79.72% for OS-Atlas and from 47.45% to 77.86% for UI-TARS, with particularly strong reductions in unnecessary toggling.

The component ablations provide evidence for explicit state reasoning: on OS-Atlas, the full method achieves 79.72% O-AMR versus 73.39% without perceiving and 73.94% without analyzing. Evaluation also includes several prompting baselines, three general agentic benchmarks, and an interactive emulator.

The approach is simple and potentially practical, requiring no auxiliary annotator at inference. The appendix supplies prompts, training hyperparameters, metric definitions, and dynamic task descriptions.
weaknesses: The principal attribution concern is the absence of a matched action-only fine-tuning baseline using the same data and training budget. StaR adds 73,652 balanced toggle examples and further training on three agentic datasets, whereas the main comparisons are against untuned or prompted models. Table 10 supports retaining both reasoning components but does not establish how much of the overall gain comes from reasoning supervision rather than learning the previously underrepresented no-action response. This is consequential because the methodological novelty is otherwise a straightforward structured reasoning template.

Benchmark independence is insufficiently established. Appendix A.1 correctly keeps opposite-instruction pairs together, but does not describe grouping by source screenshot, trajectory, or app, or deduplication across source datasets. Multiple widgets are extracted from individual screenshots, and AITW supplies over 92% of the benchmark. AITZ also derives from AITW and is used for training and evaluation. These relationships require an explicit overlap audit; the manuscript does not establish leakage, but neither does it adequately establish independent generalization.

The benchmark's label reliability is a material limitation: manual verification finds only 91% state accuracy and 92.5% functionality accuracy on 200 samples, without a reported audit of bounding-box correctness. State errors reverse the intended click/completion labels. The theoretical agreement argument in Appendix A.1 assumes independent annotator errors without validating that assumption, and its binary-error formula does not directly justify free-form functionality agreement. A verified test set would substantially strengthen the central benchmark contribution.

The generalization claims exceed the controls. AndroidControl-L supplies StaR-trained models with refined reasoning while baselines receive low-level instructions, changing test-time information as well as training. Further training on the general benchmarks also confounds attribution of their gains to StaR. Figure 7 and Appendix B.2 acknowledge AgentCPM degradations, contradicting the broad claim of consistently preserving performance. The dynamic results are encouraging, but comprise only 20 tasks without repeated-run uncertainty; UI-TARS improves by just one successful task.

Several correctable technical and reporting issues weaken precision: Eq. (1) accepts agreement on non-toggles despite the stated requirement that both annotators identify a toggle; the GUI-Owl improvement is 24.03 percentage points in Table 1 but 21.64 in the text; and Figure 6 gives the MMS example a click outside its stated bounding box. More broadly, describing selected oracle-state prompting baselines as a theoretical upper bound on training-free methods is unjustified. These issues are secondary to the missing training control and benchmark-validity concerns, which determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and practically relevant GUI failure mode: agents unnecessarily toggle controls whose current state already satisfies the instruction. The paired click/completion benchmark and separate false-positive, false-negative, and grounding metrics make this behavior easier to diagnose.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements across four agent architectures. O-AMR increases from 43.95% to 79.72% for OS-Atlas and from 47.45% to 77.86% for UI-TARS, while negative-instruction accuracy reaches approximately 96–97%. These are meaningful improvements in avoiding unwanted actions.

The component ablations provide some evidence for explicit state reasoning: OS-Atlas achieves 79.72% O-AMR with the complete reasoning chain, versus 73.39% without perceiving and 73.94% without analyzing. The appendix also includes several prompting controls, including ground-truth-state prompts.

Evaluation includes static agentic benchmarks and executable tasks. Dynamic success improves from 10% to 55% for OS-Atlas and from 20% to 42.5% for AgentCPM. The supplied prompts, hyperparameters, metric definitions, and task templates support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The principal methodological claim is insufficiently isolated from additional supervised training. StaR trains on 73,652 toggle examples plus substantial AndroidControl, AITZ, and GUI-Odyssey data, whereas the main comparisons use existing checkpoints or prompting. There is no matched training baseline using the same examples and compute with action-only supervision or ordinary reasoning. Table 10 establishes an advantage over partially removed reasoning chains, but does not establish how much of the total gain requires StaR rather than learning balanced click/completion examples. This is consequential because the method itself is a relatively simple structured supervision scheme.

Benchmark independence is incompletely documented. Appendix A.1 appropriately keeps each positive/negative pair within one split, but does not establish screenshot-, trajectory-, or app-level separation, or deduplication of multiple widgets and repeated screens. Table 3 shows that over 92% of the test examples come from AITW; AITZ is also derived from AITW. Without overlap accounting, the extent of generalization beyond familiar screens and trajectories remains uncertain. This is a risk in the reported protocol, not evidence that leakage definitely occurred.

The benchmark audit finds only 91% state accuracy and 92.5% functionality accuracy on 200 examples. Incorrect state labels reverse the required click/completion decision for both paired instructions, making this consequential evaluation noise. No manually corrected test-set results or sensitivity analysis are reported. Moreover, Equation 5 assumes independent annotation errors and a shared wrong outcome; it does not generally justify reliability for joint state/functionality annotations from two potentially correlated models.

The general-agent results do not cleanly establish the claimed preservation or improvement of capability. Additional training on the evaluated benchmarks' training splits is a confound, and AndroidControl-L supplies StaR-refined Thought inputs to trained agents while baselines receive low-level instructions, changing both the model and its input. Figure 7 also shows AgentCPM regressions on AITZ and GUI-Odyssey. Attributing these to coordinate drift does not remove them from the overall assessment. Static trajectory matching should also be distinguished from successful execution in an interactive environment.

The dynamic evaluation is encouraging but limited to 20 tasks, with no repeated-run uncertainty reported. UI-TARS improves from seven to eight successful tasks, so the evidence is considerably weaker for that model than for OS-Atlas. These results support preliminary applicability, but not the manuscript's broad language about consistently substantial real-world improvements.

Several claims and reporting details need correction. Ground-truth-state prompting is not a theoretical upper bound on all training-free or multi-agent approaches, which could also provide localization or verification. Equations 1 and 3 retain agreement on non-toggles as written, contrary to the stated filtering rule. Figure 6 gives the MMS example a click coordinate outside its listed bounding box, and the GUI-Owl improvement in Section 5.2 disagrees with Table 1. These are individually correctable issues; my weak-reject recommendation is driven primarily by the missing matched training control and unresolved evaluation validity, despite the useful problem formulation and substantial reported gains.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful, concrete failure mode in visual GUI agents: executing a toggle instruction even when the requested state already holds. The paired opposite instructions and separate grounding, false-positive, and false-negative metrics provide a useful diagnostic beyond aggregate task accuracy.

The improvements are substantial across four agents. Table 1 reports overall action accuracy increasing from 43.95% to 79.72% for OS-Atlas and from 47.45% to 77.86% for UI-TARS. Accuracy on instructions requiring no toggle reaches approximately 96–97% across all four trained agents.

The component ablations provide evidence for the structured reasoning design. In Table 10, removing perception or desired-state analysis reduces OS-Atlas accuracy from 79.72% to 73.39% or 73.94%, respectively. These comparisons support a contribution beyond merely comparing trained models against zero-shot baselines.

Evaluation includes multiple model families, three additional static benchmarks, and executable tasks in an Android emulator. The dynamic improvements for OS-Atlas, from 10% to 55%, and AgentCPM, from 20% to 42.5%, are encouraging. The appendix supplies prompts, training hyperparameters, action-matching rules, and task templates.
weaknesses: The central attribution remains incomplete. StaR combines additional balanced toggle supervision, structured reasoning targets, and further training on three agentic datasets. There is no matched action-only fine-tuning baseline or continued-training baseline using the original reasoning targets. The component ablations are helpful but retain substantial StaR structure. Consequently, the full gains cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed reasoning method, whose technical novelty is otherwise modest.

Benchmark reliability and independence need stronger support. The human audit finds only 91% state-label accuracy and 92.5% functionality accuracy, without reporting performance on a human-corrected test subset. Appendix A.1 appropriately keeps opposite-instruction pairs together, but does not establish screenshot-, trajectory-, or app-level separation or cross-dataset deduplication. This matters because several toggles can come from one screenshot, approximately 92% of test samples derive from AITW, and AITZ also derives from AITW. These are unresolved contamination risks, not demonstrated leakage.

Some generalization comparisons are confounded or overstated. In AndroidControl-L, StaR models receive refined reasoning while baseline models receive low-level instructions, so the input information is not held constant. All three agentic datasets also receive additional training exposure. Figure 7 shows AgentCPM regressions on AITZ and GUI-Odyssey; attributing these to grounding sensitivity does not support the blanket claim that general capability is preserved.

The dynamic evaluation is promising but preliminary: it contains only 20 closely related tasks, with no reported repeated trials or uncertainty estimates. UI-TARS improves from seven to eight successful tasks. These results support feasibility more strongly than broad real-world reliability.

There are correctable technical and reporting inconsistencies. Equations 1 and 3 retain agreement even when both annotators predict non-toggle, contrary to the stated filtering rule. Equation 5 assumes independent annotation errors and a binary agreement model that does not generally apply to joint state/functionality annotations. The GUI-Owl gain is 24.03 percentage points in Table 1 but 21.64 in the text.

Overall, the useful diagnostic benchmark, consistent toggle improvements, and positive component ablations place this near the acceptance boundary. However, the missing matched training controls and unresolved benchmark-validity questions prevent a confident acceptance recommendation on the evidence provided.
